title: Enteric Pathogens in children under five with diarrhoea in a rotavirus vaccinated population in Coastal Ghana, 2023.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite the introduction and wide coverage of vaccination regimes such as rotavirus vaccination globally, diarrhoea remains as a major public health problem with new studies showing an emerging pattern in its etiology. We assessed the etiology of diarrhoea in a population of children under five years appropriately vaccinated against rotavirus. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study of children under five years reporting with diarrhoea at the district health facility in the Anloga district, Ghana. Stool samples of diarrhoea cases were tested for pathogens and co-infections using standard ELISA methods and TAQMAN Array Card RT-PCR Technology. The Vesikari Clinical Severity Scoring System was used to classify diarrhoea severity. Data generated was described descriptively. RESULTS: Median age was 21.5 (IQR:12,30)months, 55.3%(21/38) with being male. About half of the cases were moderate diarrhoea severity (20/38). The Rotavirus A prevalence was 2.5%. The pathogen with the highest prevalence was Enteroaggregative Escherichia coli (EAEC) (52.6%, 20/38), Shigella/ Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli (Shigella/EIEC (76.3%, 29/38), Norovirus (26.3%, 10/38) and Giardia was the main parasite identified. The rate of co-infection was high (94.7%, 36/38). Co-infections with bacteria-virus present had more moderate-severe diarrhoea cases (73.3%, 11/15). Norovirus was present in most of the severe cases (75%, 3/4). CONCLUSION: The leading diarrhoea pathogens found were EAEC, Shigella/EIEC and Norovirus. The rate of pathogen co-infection was very high with bacteria-virus related co-infections affecting diarrhoea severity. The study recommends periodic diarrhoea pathogen surveillance through Ghana Health Service collaborating with research institutions such as Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research (NMIMR). Also, enhancing water, sanitation and hygiene practices at the district, community and individual levels as a means of diarrhoea prevention in the absence of additional vaccines for other diarrhoea pathogens.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the etiology of diarrhoea in children under five years in a rotavirus vaccinated population in Coastal Ghana. The research aimed to identify the leading pathogens causing diarrhoea and assess the impact of co-infections. Stool samples were tested using ELISA and RT-PCR methods, revealing that Norovirus had a prevalence of 26.3%, while Enteroaggregative Escherichia coli (EAEC) and Shigella/EIEC were the most common pathogens. Co-infections were prevalent, with 94.7% of cases involving multiple pathogens, and these co-infections were associated with more severe diarrhoea. The findings highlight the need for targeted surveillance and improved hygiene practices to address diarrhoea in the absence of vaccines for other pathogens. The study's results are descriptive and do not provide detailed statistical analysis, which may limit the confidence in the conclusions.

title: Treatment With Ruxolitinib and TAK-779 Enhances GII.17 Human Norovirus Replication and Enables Serial Passaging in Human Intestinal Enteroids.
abstract: Human norovirus (HuNoV) is a major cause of acute viral gastroenteritis. Although it can be replicated in vitro using human intestinal enteroids (HIEs), generating high-titer viral laboratory stocks remains challenging due to low infection and passage efficiencies. Interferon response and chemokine signaling may be key host pathways that restrict efficient HuNoV replication. Here, we evaluated the effect of their inhibitors, ruxolitinib-a Janus kinase (JAK) 1/JAK2 inhibitor-and TAK-779-a C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 3 (CXCR3)/C-C motif chemokine receptor (CCR) 5/CCR2 antagonist-on HuNoV replication in wild-type jejunal HIEs. TAK-779 increased GII.17 HuNoV replication by 2.3- and 6.0-fold at 48 and 96 h postinfection (hpi), respectively, compared with the DMSO-treated control. In contrast, ruxolitinib alone did not affect viral replication. Notably, simultaneous treatment with these compounds further enhanced GII.17 replication by 6.0- and 10.7-fold at 48 and 96 hpi, respectively, which enabled serial passaging. These findings imply that the simultaneous suppression of these pathways potentially benefits GII.17 HuNoV replication.

title: Zymosan-adjuvanted intranasal norovirus virus-like particle vaccine induces antiviral mucosal immune responses in infant mice.
abstract: Infants require repeated immunizations of injectable-type vaccines against different pathogens because their immune systems are weaker than those of adults. However, these injectable vaccines cause physical and psychological discomfort. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop pain-free mucosal vaccines that are optimized for immunologically immature infants. Using an infant murine model, we examined the effectiveness of an intranasal norovirus virus-like-particle (VLP) vaccine with zymosan as an adjuvant. The intranasal immunization of infant mice with VLPs alone induced mucosal and systemic VLP-specific immune responses that were substantially weaker than those of adults. In contrast, infant mice administered a minimum dose of intranasal zymosan-adjuvanted VLP vaccine showed increased levels of intestinal and salivary VLP-specific IgA antibodies, as well as plasma VLP-specific IgG antibodies, at levels comparable to those in adults. Importantly, intestinal and salivary antibodies elicited by intranasal immunization with the zymosan-adjuvanted VLP vaccine effectively inhibited norovirus propagation in human-induced pluripotent stem cellderived intestinal epithelial cells. These findings suggest that the intranasal zymosan-adjuvanted norovirus VLP vaccine is an effective mucosal vaccine candidate for infants. It may help reduce the pain associated with injections and the number of immunizations infants required to achieve sufficient protective immunity against norovirus.

title: Detection of Norovirus in Children 0-5 Years Presenting with Acute Diarrhoea in Three Selected Tertiary Health Facilities in Jos, Plateau State, Nigeria
abstract: Norovirus is a global health concern and is considered a leading cause of acute gastroenteritis across all age groups, resulting in sporadic infections and epidemic or endemic outbreaks worldwide. Human norovirus infection accounts for substantial morbidity and mortality annually, particularly among children younger than 5 years. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of norovirus and the risk factors associated with infection among children presenting with acute diarrhoea in three selected tertiary health facilities in Jos. A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among paediatric inpatients and general outpatient attendees from January to November 2020. Consenting participants were recruited using simple random sampling, and a stool sample was collected from each child. Data were analysed using STATA statistical software, version 15. Norovirus antigen was detected in 61 of 184 samples using the MyBioSource Norovirus Antigen enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, giving an overall prevalence of 33.2%. Plateau State Specialist Hospital accounted for the largest proportion of positive cases (68.9%), and the difference by facility was statistically significant. Among positive cases, 62.3% were male and 37.7% were female, although sex was not significantly associated with infection. The highest proportion of infections occurred among children aged 7–12 months (32.8%). Norovirus was detected throughout the study period, with the highest monthly proportion recorded in March (34.4%). Body temperature was significantly associated with norovirus infection, with 45.9% of positive cases occurring among children with temperatures of 38.0–38.9°C. The observed prevalence highlights the need to strengthen norovirus prevention, surveillance, and control interventions in Jos and to support evidence-informed consideration of future vaccination strategies. It is recommended that children and parents practice hand hygiene by washing frequently with soap and water, properly disinfect contaminated surfaces using bleach-based cleaners, and thoroughly wash fruits and vegetables before consumption to reduce risk of norovirus infection.

title_zh: 尼日利亚乔斯市高原州三家选定三级医疗机构中0-5岁儿童急性腹泻患者诺如病毒检测

Human norovirus infection accounts for substantial morbidity and mortality annually, particularly among children younger than 5 years. A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among paediatric inpatients and general outpatient attendees from January to November 2020. title: Wastewater and Environmental Surveillance in Cities with Sewered and Non-sewered Sanitation: Evidence from Kampala, Uganda
abstract: Summary Background: Wastewater and environmental surveillance (WES) enables community-level monitoring of infectious diseases. Most progress has focused on sewer-based surveillance, yet nearly half of the global population relies on non-sewered sanitation. In non-sewered settings, urban drainage channels have been used for poliovirus environmental surveillance, but their potential for a multi-pathogen WES with spatially defined catchments, and comparability to sewer-based surveillance, remains under-explored. Methods: Ten drainage channel sampling points with delineated micro-catchments (0.95-3.83 km2 with 12,885-44,146 people) were selected within Kampala. A total of 255 drainage channel and 54 wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) influent samples were collected during two campaigns in March and September-October 2025. A multi-target panel was quantified by digital PCR, including enteric viruses (Norovirus GI and GII, Rotavirus), respiratory viruses (SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A and B viruses, Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)), non-O1/O139 Vibrio cholerae (V. cholerae), and Pepper Mild Mottle Virus (PMMoV) as a fecal indicator. Findings: Enteric viruses, non-O1/O139 V. cholerae, and PMMoV were consistently detected across all drainage channels and WWTP influents. Concentrations were generally lower in drainage than WWTP influents, except for non-O1/O139 V. When normalized by PMMoV, concentrations across most drainage channels were comparable to WWTP influents, although comparability varied by target and location. Both concentrations and PMMoV-normalized concentrations varied across sampling locations. Trends between campaigns varied by pathogen target and were not explained by any single micro-catchment characteristic. Influenza A virus was the most frequently detected respiratory virus (8-23% in drainage channels; 3-10% in WWTP influents), while SARS-CoV-2, Influenza B, and RSV were rarely detected. Interpretation: PMMoV-normalized concentrations across most micro-catchments were comparable to WWTP influents, with spatial heterogeneity implying neighborhood-level differences in disease prevalence. Catchment-delineated drainage surveillance has potential to offer spatially resolved public health information in non-sewered settings comparable to sewer-based wastewater monitoring. Funding: Eawag Discretionary Funding

The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations and the absence of detailed causal interpretations.

title: Microbial assessment of recontamination with multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter in patient room environment in a burn unit.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Numerous studies have demonstrated that environmental contamination with several epidemiologically important pathogens, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus spp, Acinetobacter, norovirus, and Clostridioides difficile, can persist for several days to months and contributes to the transmission of these pathogens. METHODS: This study was conducted in a burn intensive care unit to determine the time to recontamination of environmental surfaces with a multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii after disinfection. After disinfection, samples were taken from 6 environmental sites using Rodac plates at 1-hour intervals for 10 hours. RESULTS: Time to recontamination with Acinetobacter was as follows: chair, 3 hours; overbed table, 2 hours; stock cabinet, 3 hours; and IV pump, 2 hours. CONCLUSIONS: Our study demonstrated that recontamination with Acinetobacter occurred rapidly at environmental sites in burn units even after cleaning/disinfection and underscored the need for enhanced environmental cleaning, including continuous disinfection methods, to prevent transmission of health care-associated pathogens.

Six high-touch surfaces were sampled hourly for 10 hours using Rodac plates. Recontamination occurred within 2–3 hours on all sampled sites, demonstrating that surfaces become recontaminated quickly even after cleaning. The authors interpreted these results as evidence that conventional disinfection is insufficient and that continuous or enhanced environmental cleaning is necessary to prevent transmission. The findings imply that burn units should adopt continuous disinfection strategies to reduce healthcare-associated Acinetobacter transmission. However, the study’s single-centre design, short follow-up, and lack of patient outcome data limit generalisability and strength of evidence.

title: Detection Patterns and Temporal Dynamics of Multiple Pathogens in Wastewater Using a TaqMan Array Card
abstract: Background: Wastewater-based surveillance (WBS) complements clinical surveillance by capturing community-level circulation of infectious diseases, including asymptomatic infections.However, most multipathogen WBS studies have focused on pathogen detection and detection frequency, with limited evaluation of temporal changes using semi-quantitative Ct values.Objectives: This study aimed to characterize multipathogen detection patterns in wastewater using a customdesigned TaqMan Array Card (TAC) and explore temporal changes using semi-quantitative Ct values.Methods: Weekly influent samples (500 mL) were collected from two wastewater treatment plants in Cheonan and Asan during weeks 21~52 of 2025 (64 total samples).The TAC targeted 31 pathogen analysis groups encompassing respiratory, enteric, and selected high-concern pathogens, along with seven antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs).Pathogen occurrence was evaluated based on week-based detection status and detection frequency, while Ct values were interpreted as a semi-quantitative indicator for exploratory assessment of temporal changes.Samples failing the predefined quality control criteria were re-extracted and reanalyzed, and all samples were ultimately included in the final analysis.Results: Ten pathogens, including SARS-CoV-2, norovirus, adenovirus type F, and human rhinovirus, were detected in 100% of the study weeks.Influenza A virus and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) showed increased detection during winter, with influenza A/H3 and RSV type B predominating among their respective subtypes.Semi-quantitative Ct values showed no consistent increasing or decreasing trend for SARS-CoV-2, but they declined during winter for norovirus and influenza A. In contrast, RSV showed increased winter detection without a corresponding decrease in Ct values.bla_KPC, bla_NDM, and vanA/B/ C were detected in all study weeks, and mecA and bla_OXA also showed high detection frequencies.Conclusions: TAC-based WBS enabled simultaneous characterization of multipathogen detection patterns, antimicrobial resistance gene detection, and exploratory assessment of temporal changes using semiquantitative Ct values.These findings support TAC-based WBS as an integrated tool for community-level infectious disease surveillance.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to characterize multipathogen detection patterns in wastewater using a TaqMan Array Card (TAC) and explore temporal changes using semi-quantitative Ct values. Weekly influent samples were collected from two wastewater treatment plants in Cheonan and Asan during weeks 21~52 of 2025, targeting 31 pathogens and seven antimicrobial resistance genes. The results showed that norovirus was detected in all study weeks, with semi-quantitative Ct values declining during winter. The findings support TAC-based wastewater-based surveillance as a tool for community-level infectious disease monitoring, particularly for tracking norovirus and other pathogens with seasonal variations. However, the study's limitations include the lack of subtype-specific analysis and the potential imprecision of Ct values in assessing temporal trends, resulting in moderate confidence in the conclusions.

title: Evolution, diversity and distribution of human Noroviruses:From single hosts to global patterns
abstract: Norovirus, a member of the Caliciviridae family, is a major cause of acute gastroenteritis (AGE) worldwide, affecting all age groups and causing substantial morbidity and mortality. Children in developing countries, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals are particularly affected. Currently, no specific antivirals or vaccines are licensed for norovirus treatment or prevention. Therapeutic development is complicated by the virus's high diversity, with more than 10 genogroups (GI–GX) and approximately 50 genotypes, some of which, such as GII.4, continuously generate new antigenic variants. However, the emergence of norovirus diversity, the relationship between within-host and community-level evolution, and the association between viral diversity and treatment outcome remain incompletely understood. Therefore, this thesis aims to improve our understanding of norovirus evolution and epidemiology by addressing two main topics: norovirus diversity and evolution in different hosts, and the use of wastewater-based sequencing to monitor viral diversity and circulation at the population level.

title: Colorimetric-Catalytic-SERS Trimodal Immunochromatographic Assay for Multi-Scenario Monitoring of Gastrointestinal Infections.
abstract: Direct pathogen detection in stool samples is the gold standard for diagnosing gastrointestinal infections, yet substantial technical challenges remain. Here, we report a versatile immunochromatographic assay (ICA) for simultaneous detection of both bacteria and virus, integrating a trimodal readout strategy combining magnetic enrichment with colorimetric, catalytic, and surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) signals. We developed a self-assembled magnetic SERS nanozyme by electrostatically layer-by-layer depositing multilayer PtIr nanoparticles and Au nanostars onto a magnetic core, affording strong peroxidase-like activity and electromagnetic enhancement. In addition, a multi-feature fusion neural-network model was designed for intelligent SERS signal analysis, enabling accurate quantification of pathogen concentrations. The method exhibits high analytical performance across all three modalities: in colorimetric mode, the visual limits of detection (vLODs) were 5 × 103 CFU/mL for Escherichia coli O157 and 0.05 ng/mL for norovirus; in catalytic mode, a 2 min substrate-catalysis step reduced the colorimetric vLOD by 100-fold; in SERS mode, the detection limits were further lowered to 8 CFU/mL and 0.11 pg/mL via a quantitative algorithm. Application to 116 clinical stool samples showed detection rates consistent with quantitative real-time PCR, while reducing the assay time to 1/8. Therefore, this trimodal ICA holds strong potential for rapid and accurate detection of gastrointestinal infections across diverse scenarios.

title: Simplified Linear Dose‐Response Models for Low‐Dose QMRAs
abstract: ABSTRACT This study analyzes widely used dose‐response (DR) models from potable reuse quantitative microbial risk assessments (QMRAs) to identify the low‐dose ranges where the log 10 ‐transformed probability of infection and pathogen dose exhibit a linear relationship. Target pathogens include norovirus, adenovirus, enterovirus, Cryptosporidium , and Giardia . This study (i) defines the low‐dose linear range for each DR model, (ii) extracts slope and intercept parameters via regression, and (iii) shows that municipal drinking water risk thresholds fall within these ranges. This promotes low‐dose risk estimation transparency, reproducibility, and accessibility for utility decision making, regardless of the underlying complexity of the DR model. Also, this study shows that within the low‐dose ranges relevant to potable reuse, commonly used DR models exhibit linear relationships with a slope of ~1. Therefore, each 10‐fold reduction in pathogen concentration, equivalent to one log reduction value (LRV), reduces risk by a corresponding order of magnitude. Finally, the outputs from the various DR models are separated by relatively constant risk differentials, thereby reducing the need for complex DR‐based sensitivity analyses when conducting potable reuse QMRAs.

title: Viral gastroenteritis: Molecular epidemiology of human norovirus by RT-PCR at University Hospital Center of Brazzaville, Republic of Congo
abstract: Acute gastroenteritis (AGE) is a major public health concern in Africa, with noroviruses (NoV) recognized as the predominant viral etiological agents. However, their epidemiological impact remains underreported in the Republic of Congo, particularly in Brazzaville. This study aimed to determine the molecular prevalence of NoV among children presenting with AGE, identify the circulating genogroups, and evaluate associated sociodemographic and clinical factors. A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted from June to November 2020 at the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville. Fifty children aged 28 days to 17 years presenting with AGE were enrolled. Stool samples were analyzed using real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) to detect viral RNA and differentiate between GI and GII genogroups. Eighty percent were aged ≤5 years. The overall prevalence of NoV infection was 44%, with GII (73%) predominating over GI (18%). GI/GII co-infections were detected in 9% of cases. Clinically, fever was reported in 80% of cases, increased stool frequency in 86%, and dehydration was observed in all participants (100%). A significant association was observed between age and NoV genogroup distribution (p = 0.03), with GII being more prevalent among children aged ≤5 years. However, clinical manifestations did not differ significantly between genogroups (p > 0.05). Norovirus represents an important cause of pediatric AGE in Brazzaville. Socioeconomic conditions and inadequate hygiene practices appear to play significant roles in NoV transmission.The integration of molecular diagnostic approaches into national surveillance programs and the strengthening of sanitation measures are recommended to improve prevention and control strategies. Key words: Norovirus, acute gastroenteritis, molecular epidemiology, reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), Congo.

INTRODUCTION Noroviruses (NoV) are non-enveloped, single-stranded RNA viruses belonging to the family Caliciviridae and are 2 J. Gen. Mol. Virol. recognized as the leading etiological agents of acute viral gastroenteritis (AGE) worldwide (Winder et al., 2022). They are responsible for a substantial proportion of sporadic and epidemic gastroenteritis cases across all age groups and contribute significantly to morbidity and mortality, particularly among young children, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals (Troeger et al., 2017). Due to their low infectious dose, prolonged environmental persistence, and high transmissibility, NoV infections represent a major global public health concern (World Health Organization (WHO), 2024; Patel et al., 2009). Diarrheal diseases remain among the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in children under five years of age, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Recent estimates indicate that AGE accounts for hundreds of thousands of childhood deaths annually, with the highest disease burden occurring in Africa and South Asia (Sarno et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2017). Following the widespread introduction of rotavirus vaccines, the epidemiology of viral gastroenteritis has changed considerably, with norovirus emerging as the predominant viral cause of AGE in many regions worldwide (Cates et al., 2022; Dakouo et al., 2024; Chilaúle et al., 2022). In sub-Saharan Africa, norovirus infections represent an increasing public health challenge. Several studies conducted in Burkina Faso, Mozambique, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Gabon, and Cameroon have reported substantial prevalence rates among children presenting with acute diarrhea (Dakouo et al., 2024; Chilaúle et al., 2022; Afework et al., 2022; Louya et al., 2019; Rönnelid et al., 2020; Tegegne et al., 2024). However, the true burden of norovirus infection in the region remains underestimated due to limited access to molecular diagnostic methods, inadequate laboratory infrastructure, weak surveillance systems, and underreporting of gastroenteritis cases. These challenges hinder accurate estimation of disease burden and the development of effective prevention and control strategies. In developing countries, poor sanitation, limited access to safe drinking water, overcrowding, and inadequate healthcare resources contribute substantially to the transmission of enteric viruses, including NoV (Rönnelid et al., 2020). In the Republic of Congo, only a limited number of studies have investigated the epidemiology of norovirus infections. A previous study conducted in Brazzaville reported a prevalence of approximately 27% among hospitalized children with acute diarrhea (Ndjangangoye et al., 2023). Nevertheless, available epidemiological data remain scarce and fragmented. In 2020, the Republic of the Congo experienced an increase in cases of acute diarrheal disease, particularly among children requiring hospital care. Globally, norovirus had already emerged as the leading viral cause of epidemic AGE following the widespread implementation of rotavirus vaccination programs. However, despite this epidemiological context, molecular epidemiological data describing circulating norovirus genogroups were unavailable in the Republic of Congo. Therefore, documenting norovirus circulation during this period represented an important public health priority and provided baseline epidemiological information for the country (Cates et al., 2022; Dakouo et al., 2024; Chilaúle et al., 2022; Lopman et al., 2022). Ideally, effective surveillance systems supported by routine molecular diagnostic testing would enable continuous monitoring of circulating norovirus strains, early detection of outbreaks, and implementation of evidence-based public health interventions. However, in the Republic of the Congo, routine laboratory diagnosis of norovirus is not widely available, and epidemiological surveillance remains limited. Consequently, information regarding circulating geno- groups, transmission patterns, and associated risk factors remains insufficient. This lack of epidemiological information may have important public health implications, including delayed outbreak detection, inadequate allocation of healthcare resources, reduced effectiveness of preventive inter- ventions, and limited preparedness for future vaccine implementation programs. Strengthening local epidemio- logical evidence is therefore essential for improving disease control strategies and informing national health policies. Therefore, the present study aimed to determine the molecular prevalence of norovirus among children presenting with acute gastroenteritis at the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville, identify the circulating genogroups, and evaluate associated sociodemographic and clinical factors. By addressing existing knowledge gaps, this study seeks to provide valuable epidemio- logical evidence to support norovirus surveillance, prevention, and control strategies in the Republic of Congo. MATERIALS AND METHODS Ethics statement This study was approved by the Health Sciences Research Ethics Committee of the Republic of the Congo (Reference No. 286/MRSIT/IRSSA/CERSSA). Study population A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted from June 1 to November 1, 2020, in the Pediatric Emergency Department of the University Hospital Center of Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo. The study population consisted of children aged between 28 days and 17 years presenting with acute gastroenteritis during the study period, regardless of their immunological status. Acute gastroenteritis was defined as the passage of three or more loose or watery stools within a 24-h period. Children younger than 28 days of age, those presenting with bloody or mucoid diarrhea, and those with chronic or prolonged gastroenteritis were excluded from the study. The inclusion of a broad pediatric age range (28 days to 17 years) was intended to provide a comprehensive assessment of norovirus circulation across the pediatric population attending the referral hospital. Although norovirus infections are more frequently reported among children under five years of age, older children may also contribute to transmission dynamics and disease burden. Sample collection Participants were recruited using a consecutive sampling strategy. All eligible children presenting during the study period were enrolled consecutively until the target sample size was reached. The sample size of 50 participants corresponded to all eligible patients recruited during the study period and reflected the logistical and financial constraints associated with molecular testing. Although relatively small, this sample provided preliminary epidemiological data on norovirus infections among children with acute gastroenteritis in Brazzaville. A structured questionnaire was administered to collect sociodemographic, environmental, and clinical information. Stool samples were collected from all enrolled participants and transported under appropriate conditions to the laboratory. Samples were stored at −80°C until molecular analysis. RNA extraction RNA extraction was performed using the Stool Total RNA Purification Kit Dx (NORGEN BIOTEK CORPORATION, Canada), following the manufacturer's instructions. This method is designed for isolation and purification of high-quality total RNA from stool samples, and based on spin column chromatography using Norgen’s proprietary resin as the separation matrix. RNA extracts were stored at -20°C prior to NoV detection and genogroup identification. The assay differentiates genogroups GI and GII using genotype-specific primers and hydrolysis probes labeled with distinct fluorescent dyes. Detection of fluorescence in the GI channel alone was interpreted as GI infection, whereas fluorescence detected only in the GII channel indicated GII infection. Simultaneous amplification in both channels, Amona et al. 3 together with valid internal and external controls, was interpreted as a mixed GI/GII infection according to the manufacturer's instructions. Positive and negative controls provided by the manufacturer were included in each RT-PCR run to ensure assay reliability. Associations between categorical variables were assessed using the Chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test when appropriate. Continuous variables were compared using Student’s t-test. Statistical significance was defined as a p-value < 0.05. They are responsible for a substantial proportion of sporadic and epidemic gastroenteritis cases across all age groups and contribute significantly to morbidity and mortality, particularly among young children, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals (Troeger et al., 2017). Due to their low infectious dose, prolonged environmental persistence, and high transmissibility, NoV infections represent a major global public health concern (World Health Organization (WHO), 2024; Patel et al., 2009). Diarrheal diseases remain among the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in children under five years of age, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Recent estimates indicate that AGE accounts for hundreds of thousands of childhood deaths annually, with the highest disease burden occurring in Africa and South Asia (Sarno et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2017). These challenges hinder accurate estimation of disease burden and the development of effective prevention and control strategies.
